plan.title: How GPS Works: Time into Position
plan.hook: A GPS receiver solves a timing problem using moving reference points. See why four satellites matter and why extra decimal places do not guarantee accuracy.
objectives: Convert signal timing error to range error.
Identify the four unknowns in a basic position fix.
Separate accuracy, repeatability and display resolution.

sections.heading: Tiny time errors become large distances
sections.body:
GPS satellites broadcast information that lets a receiver estimate satellite position and signal transmission time. Comparing transmit and receive times gives apparent travel time. Multiplying by signal speed turns that interval into a range estimate.

Radio signals travel at about 300 million metres per second in vacuum. One microsecond—one millionth of a second—therefore corresponds to roughly 300 metres. Even 10 nanoseconds corresponds to about 3 metres. Timing precision is central to the measurement, not a finishing touch added after locating the receiver.

The initial measurement is a pseudorange because it includes errors such as receiver-clock offset and atmospheric delays. The receiver listens to one-way satellite broadcasts; it does not have to transmit a ranging request back to each satellite. A phone may also use network assistance, which is a separate part of its positioning system.
sections.visual: Picture timestamped lighthouse flashes from known moving locations. Your receiver compares each flash's travel time to the speed of light to get a range.

questions.q: Approximately how much range error corresponds to a 1 microsecond timing error?
questions.hint: Multiply 300 million m/s by one millionth of a second.
questions.answer: About 300 m. Small timing errors become large range errors because radio signals travel so quickly.

sections.heading: Three coordinates plus one clock
sections.body:
If the receiver clock were exact, a known satellite range would constrain position to a sphere. More independent ranges narrow the possibilities. Real receivers must estimate their own clock offset as well as location, so the standard unconstrained three-dimensional problem has four unknowns: three position coordinates and one clock offset.

At least four suitably placed satellites are normally required for that basic solution. Additional measurements provide redundancy and can improve estimation. Special systems with extra constraints can behave differently, so the four-satellite rule is not a statement about every possible navigation method.

Geometry matters too. Reference points spread across the sky generally constrain different directions better than points clustered together. Poor geometry can amplify a small range error into a large position error. A high satellite count alone is therefore not a complete quality measure: the arrangement and trustworthiness of those measurements matter.
sections.visual: Picture several translucent range spheres meeting near a receiver. Adjusting its clock until the spheres agree gives both position and time offset.

questions.q: Why does the fourth satellite add useful information?
questions.answer: The basic unconstrained solution estimates the receiver-clock offset alongside three coordinates, giving four unknown quantities.

sections.heading: More digits do not guarantee a better fix
sections.body:
Accuracy means closeness to the true position. Repeatability describes how tightly repeated estimates cluster, and display resolution describes how finely a number is shown. A tight cluster can still be systematically displaced, while extra decimal places can simply decorate a noisy estimate.

Atmospheric effects, imperfect satellite information, receiver noise and reflected signals all affect ranges. Multipath occurs when a signal reaches the receiver by an indirect route, such as a reflection from a building. That extra route can distort the range estimate even though the receiver itself did not move.

Correction methods can estimate and reduce particular errors, while advanced signal measurements can support much greater precision. They do not remove every obstruction, reflection or geometry problem. When evaluating a guidance display, consider solution quality and measurement conditions as well as the coordinates. A sudden shift near a wall is a reason to inspect the measurement, not assume the mapped feature physically moved.
sections.visual: Picture tightly grouped darts away from a target centre: repeatable but biased. GPS errors from clock, atmosphere, and geometry act the same way — precision is not accuracy.

questions.q: What does adding decimal places definitely change?
questions.hint: Separate a displayed representation from a measurement.
questions.answer: It changes display resolution. It does not by itself improve the physical measurement or absolute accuracy.

questions.q: What range error corresponds approximately to 10 nanoseconds?
questions.explain: 10 ns = 0.00000001 s. Multiplying by about 300,000,000 m/s gives 3 m.

questions.q: How does a basic GPS receiver obtain satellite ranging signals?
choices: It queries each satellite with a radio message
questions.explain: The basic ranging principle uses one-way broadcasts. Network assistance is distinct from having to query GPS satellites.

questions.q: Which set contains the standard four unknowns?
choices: Latitude, longitude, fuel and tyre size
questions.explain: Clock offset is estimated along with the receiver’s three position coordinates.

questions.q: With similar range noise and satellite count, which geometry is generally better?
choices: Satellites well spread across the sky
questions.explain: Well-spread geometry constrains multiple directions more effectively. Clustered satellites can leave some directions poorly determined.

questions.q: A reflected signal travels farther before reaching the receiver. What can result?
questions.explain: An indirect route can bias the apparent travel time and range. The receiver need not have moved.

questions.q: Repeated coordinates cluster tightly but are all displaced from the true location. Which description fits?
questions.explain: Tight clustering demonstrates repeatability under those conditions, while the shared displacement indicates an accuracy problem.
